summary.title: Your configs suck? Try a real programming language.
summary.one_liner: Learn why plain config formats like JSON, YAML, TOML and INI frustrate people, and when writing configs in a general-purpose language such as Python is a practical alternative, with its trade-offs.
takeaways: Plain config formats (JSON/YAML/TOML/INI) lack reuse, logic, validation and comments in many cases, forcing users to reinvent programming constructs.
A general-purpose language like Python can serve as a config: write the config as code, exec or import it, and get comments, reuse, logic and validation for free.
Code-as-config trade-offs include interoperability with other languages, harder programmatic editing, security risks from untrusted configs, and possible non-termination.
Many projects already use code for configuration (Webpack, setuptools, Emacs, Bazel/Starlark, Gradle, Awesome WM), and purpose-built languages like Dhall, Jsonnet and Cue are alternatives.
If you must use plain configs, keep CI and Dockerfile configs short, move logic into helper scripts, or generate configs from a program.
summary.summary: The author argues that most plain config formats (JSON, YAML, TOML, INI) are frustrating because they lack comments, reuse, logic, and validation, pushing users to write ad hoc tooling anyway. He proposes writing configs in a real programming language such as Python, with a toy example of loading a config via exec, and then weighs downsides like interoperability, security, termination, and programmatic modification. The post surveys projects that use code or DSLs for configuration (Webpack, Bazel/Skylark, Emacs, Dhall, Jsonnet, Nix), and ends with practical tips for working with plain configs and a P.S. addressing common objections.
